paragraphs.heading: What an alcohol is
paragraphs.text: An alcohol is an organic compound with at least one hydroxyl group, written −OH, attached to a saturated carbon atom. The family runs from small molecules such as methanol and ethanol up to bigger ones such as cholesterol and the sugar alcohols.

paragraphs.heading: Why the OH group matters
paragraphs.text: Putting an OH group on a hydrocarbon changes how that molecule behaves in a big way. It makes the molecule hydrophilic, which means drawn to water. The OH group is also a spot where many chemical reactions can take place.

paragraphs.heading: Naming alcohols
paragraphs.text: In official names set by the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry (IUPAC), the ending -ol marks an alcohol whenever the hydroxyl group is the highest-priority group in the molecule. For a simple alcohol, the final e of the alkane chain name is dropped and -ol is added, so ethane gives ethanol. A number can show where the hydroxyl sits: propan-1-ol is CH₃CH₂CH₂OH, while propan-2-ol is CH₃CH(OH)CH₃. Molecules with more than one hydroxy group are called polyols and take endings such as -diol and -triol, as in propane-1,2-diol, also known as propylene glycol.

paragraphs.heading: Primary, secondary and tertiary
paragraphs.text: Alcohols are sorted into primary, secondary and tertiary types. The sorting counts how many carbon atoms are joined to the carbon that holds the hydroxyl group, and in casual use the types are written 1°, 2° and 3°. Everyday names often pair the alkyl group with the word alcohol, as in methyl alcohol or ethyl alcohol. So the name propyl alcohol is ambiguous: it covers both n-propyl and isopropyl alcohol, which differ in whether the hydroxyl hangs off the end carbon or the middle carbon of the straight propane chain.

paragraphs.heading: Not every OH makes an alcohol
paragraphs.text: When the hydroxy group is bonded to a carbon in an aromatic ring, the molecule goes into a separate class called phenols. Phenols have properties of their own and are not counted as alcohols. Names can also hide the group: sugars such as glucose and sucrose carry hydroxyl groups, yet their common names have neither -ol nor hydroxy-.

paragraphs.heading: From eyeliner to ethanol
paragraphs.text: The word alcohol comes from the Arabic al-kuḥl, a powder worn as eyeliner. At first the term meant a very fine powder made by subliming the mineral stibnite, used as an antiseptic and a cosmetic as well as an eyeliner. Its meaning later widened to distilled substances in general and then narrowed to ethanol. In the 18th century it came to mean spirit of wine, and after 1850 chemists stretched it to the whole class now called alcohols.

paragraphs.heading: Distilling wine
paragraphs.text: Ancient thinkers such as Aristotle, Theophrastus and Pliny the Elder already knew that the vapors of wine could catch fire. A ninth-century writing attributed to Jābir ibn Ḥayyān noted that adding salt to boiling wine could make those vapors burn more readily. By the twelfth century, Latin recipes described making aqua ardens, or burning water, by distilling wine with salt. Taddeo Alderotti later described repeated fractional distillation through a water-cooled still that could reach 90% purity.
